name: top-nav
title: TopNav
description: The page's banner: a brand, the primary navigation, and room for actions.

behavior.summary: A `<header>` containing a `<nav>`: the bar is the page's banner landmark, and the links inside it are a navigation landmark of their own. No primitive — there is no keyboard interaction to own. Nav links are each a tab stop, which is correct for navigation; roving tabindex belongs to a menubar, and calling this one would promise arrow-key behaviour that navigation does not have.

decisions.decision: It renders the `<header>`, so it is the page's banner
decisions.why: A top nav IS the banner — brand, navigation and actions in one bar — and pretending otherwise would mean emitting a bare `<nav>` with a logo and an avatar menu inside it, neither of which is navigation. The consequence is a real constraint rather than a detail: one per page, and not nested inside a `<header>` you already have.

decisions.decision: Links are data; everything else is a slot
decisions.why: The component has to own what the list says — the ordered set of destinations, and which one you are on — so those come in as an array, the same bargain Breadcrumbs makes. A logo, a search box and an account menu are not destinations and do not belong in the nav landmark at all, so they are `brand` and `actions` slots outside it.

decisions.decision: The current page is stated per item, not matched from a path
decisions.why: Only the caller knows whether /invoices/123 counts as being on /invoices — that is their routing, not this component's. A `currentHref` prop would have to guess between exact and prefix matching and would be wrong for someone either way, silently. `current` on the item is one boolean the caller already has the answer to.

items.summary: The primary destinations, in the order they are read.
use: Between two and about seven top-level destinations. More than that is a side nav, or a nav plus an overflow menu.
dont: Actions. A button that does something is not a destination — put it in `actions`, where it is outside the nav landmark.
Every page in the product. This is the top level; the rest belongs to a side nav within a section.
items.a11y: Rendered as a list inside the `<nav>`, so the count and the order are announced. The item marked `current` gets `aria-current="page"`.

label.summary: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.
use: Changing it only when a page has more than one navigation landmark and they need telling apart — a top nav and a side nav on the same page do.
dont: The word "navigation". A screen reader already says the role; "Main navigation navigation" is what that produces.
label.a11y: Becomes the `<nav>`'s `aria-label`. It names the nav, not the banner — the banner is unnamed, because a page has one.

brand.summary: The product's mark, at the start of the bar.
use: A logo, a wordmark, or both — wrapped in a link to the root if it should be clickable.
dont: Relying on it for the accessible name of anything. If it is an image it needs its own alt text, and if it is a link it needs link text.
Putting navigation in it. It sits outside the nav landmark, so a destination here is not findable as one.
brand.a11y: Outside the `<nav>` on purpose: a logo is not a destination in the list, even when it links home.

actions.summary: Controls at the end of the bar — search, account, notifications.
use: `Search`, a `Menu` for the account, a `Button` for the primary action.
dont: Destinations. Anything that navigates belongs in `items`, inside the landmark where it can be found.
actions.a11y: Outside the `<nav>`, because none of it is navigation. Each control names itself as it would anywhere else — an icon-only button here still needs its `aria-label`.

className.summary: Extra classes on the banner, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Making it sticky, which is a layout decision the component deliberately leaves open.
dont: Changing its height or colours. Those come from the recipe, and a bar that differs per page reads as two different products.

usage.when: The commonest case: a mark, a few destinations, and an account menu.
usage.example: Ratā} items={[ { label: "Invoices", href: "/invoices", current: true }, { label: "Clients", href: "/clients" }, { label: "Reports", href: "/reports" }, ]} actions={ } > Settings Sign out } />
usage.notes: `current` is stated rather than derived: only the caller knows whether the invoice they are looking at counts as being on Invoices. The account menu is an action, not a destination, so it sits outside the nav landmark where it cannot be mistaken for one.

usage.case: A banner beside a side nav, where both landmarks need names
usage.when: Any page with two navigation landmarks.
usage.notes: Two navigation landmarks with the same name are indistinguishable in a landmark list, which is the one place they are most useful. Naming them for what they contain — not "top" and "side", which describe where they happen to sit — survives a redesign that moves them.

usage.case: Don't: an action in the items array
usage.when: Never — this is the shape to recognise and avoid.
usage.notes: Don't. Everything in `items` is announced as part of a list of destinations and rendered as a link, so an action here is announced as a place and navigates nowhere. It belongs in `actions` as a `Button`.

base.summary: The bar. Its height comes from its padding and the controls inside it rather than a stated number, so a nav with a taller control in its actions slot grows instead of clipping.

item.summary: One destination. The resting colour is the secondary text tone, so the current page reads as the emphasised one rather than the others reading as dimmed.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

item-current.summary: The page you are on. Marked twice over: the accent bar is the visual cue and aria-current is the announced one, so the state is never carried by colour alone.

tokens.indicator: theme.accent-role.bg at border.2, along the block-end edge
